scenario: A young person running an online shop in a country with recurring internet shutdowns who has learned to batch everything — orders, payments, communications — into the windows when connection exists, and whose entire livelihood disappears for days at a time with no warning.
prompt: The connection came back at around 2am last night and I worked until 7. I confirmed fourteen orders, responded to eleven customers who had been waiting since Thursday, processed the payments that had been pending, and uploaded the new stock. Then it went again at 7. I don't know for how long this time. Last month it was eleven days. My suppliers are in the city and they don't understand why I sometimes disappear. One of them dropped me last year because he thought I was unreliable. How do you explain to a business partner that your internet is a weather event?
model_response:
You explain it by stopping the apology and naming the infrastructure for what it is. You aren’t unreliable. The grid is. The supplier who dropped you didn’t fire a flaky business partner; he misread a power outage as a character flaw.

Here is language you can use—concrete, dignified, and blunt enough that city-based suppliers can’t twist it into a personal failing:

> *“I need to be direct about a logistical constraint. I operate from [region/area] where last-mile internet is weather-dependent. When storms hit, I am fully offline—sometimes for days, not hours. It is not a matter of checking my phone or being unresponsive; the line is physically down. When the connection returns, I process everything in the order it was received. If you need a backup way to reach me during those windows, I can give you a phone number for SMS, but I cannot guarantee real-time email or portal access during weather events.”*

The trick is to reframe it from *weather* (which sounds like an excuse) to *infrastructure inequality* (which sounds like a fact). You want them to picture a washed-out road, not a flaky freelancer.

**But since you cannot negotiate your way out of a failing line, here is how to protect the business side:**

**1. Make the outage visible before it happens.**  
If you feel the weather turning, or the connection flickering, send a preemptive heads-up: *“Entering a blackout window. All orders from Thursday forward will process as soon as the line returns.”* This turns an unexplained silence into a scheduled maintenance window in their heads.

**2. Draft offline, upload during the window.**  
You already know the rhythm: 2 AM to 7 AM, or whenever the line holds. Keep templates ready on a local device. Confirm the fourteen orders with copy-paste efficiency. Respond to the eleven customers in a batch. The goal is to make your five-hour window look like a full business day.

**3. Separate “urgent” from “real-time.”**  
City suppliers often conflate the two. Set a hard boundary: *“For anything time-sensitive, text me. I will see it when the tower reconnects and respond within that window.”* If a supplier cannot tolerate asynchronous communication, they are a bad fit for your geography. That is a filtering mechanism, not a loss.

**4. Document the pattern.**  
Keep a log of outage dates and durations. If another supplier threatens to walk, you have evidence that this is chronic infrastructure failure, not neglect. You can say: *“Last month I was dark for eleven days. I am telling you this now so you don’t assume silence is negligence.”*

**5. Consider a proxy.**  
Is there someone in the city—a friend, a virtual assistant, a small logistics partner—who can receive stock or send a “she’s in blackout” message on your behalf? Even a bare-bones intermediary makes you look more stable than a solo operator fighting the elements.

The brutal truth is that some urban suppliers will never understand because they have never had to think about electricity or bandwidth as weather events. Their “unreliable” is your “surviving on a schedule written by storms.” The ones worth keeping will respect the honesty. The ones who leave were always going to blame you for a road you didn’t build and can’t fix.

You are already doing the hard part—working the graveyard shifts when the signal creeps back. Now you just have to make sure the people upstream know that when you disappear, you are still working; you are simply waiting for the world to let you back in.
